summary:
Arauca department sits under Colombia's national framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

That framework sits alongside lethal violence. On 5 April 2025 a video went viral showing Sara Millerey, 32, attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia; she died of a second cardiac arrest at three the following afternoon. No one has been arrested, although police interrogated local residents. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities. Thirteen trans people were killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025. Eight trans women were killed between February and April 2024, and 41 in 2023. Earlier fatal attacks recorded in the same reporting include gay men lured through an app and killed, a trans rough-sleeper stabbed while sleeping, and victims killed in their homes or in a hairdresser.

Some of the targeting is organised by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. In Caquetá department, three armed men gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, one week to leave town or be killed; she hid for a week and then fled at night. "Social cleansing" flyers appeared on Caquetá streets and via WhatsApp naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Discrimination limits trans women in Caquetá mainly to hairdressing or sex work, and trans women in that department have few options beyond sex work.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

No Arauca-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding appears in the source inventory. The violence, threat and displacement material available for this record is national and departmental evidence from Antioquia, Caquetá and Guajira, and it is presented as the pattern a visitor to Arauca should expect to be shaped by rather than as a finding about Arauca itself.
tangentialFactors:
The organised-campaign evidence comes from departments neighbouring or near Arauca in the eastern and Andean corridor. Caquetá lies south of Arauca along the same corridor of coca-growing and conflict-affected territory, and the Guardian investigation found armed groups there issuing deadline threats, publishing flyer lists and driving trans women out of towns despite the 2016 peace agreement. Guajira, in the north, shows the same tactic of named kill lists posted publicly from March 2024. Whether comparable flyer campaigns, deadline threats or "social cleansing" declarations operate inside Arauca is not sourced here.

The gap between formal protection and lived experience is the recurring finding across sources. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023, and the UN Independent Expert concluded in May 2025 that institutional progress has not reached daily life. Reporting on the Millerey case describes calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict, and killings of queer Colombians continued after that case.

Comparison points a visitor may hold in mind: Colombia's notary-based marker change contrasts with jurisdictions requiring court orders, surgery or psychiatric opinion, and the 2015 reform explicitly replaced bodily inspections and assessments. Set against that, the threat environment in Arauca's region is closer to departments where armed groups, not the state, set the terms of who may appear in public.
localsOnly:
Residents change the sex marker on national identification by signing a document before a notary, a route available since the June 2015 rule change, and identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 grounds recognition in self-recognition without a surgical requirement.

Access to public and commercial premises is protected by judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk). A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees.

The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict. A May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

For residents, the practical constraint recorded in Caquetá is economic as well as physical: discrimination confines trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work, and displacement after threats is a repeated outcome, as in the case of trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes, forced to move twice.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Arauca-specific source was available for this record. Whether Arauca department has recorded trans homicides, threat flyers, forced displacement of trans residents, or departmental enforcement of the national marker-change route is unresolved and not sourced here.

The status of a comprehensive trans legislative bill is not sourced in this inventory; the current summary's reference to such a bill could not be verified against the claims provided and is left open.

Figures for trans killings differ by period and by recording body: 13 in the first quarter of 2025, 8 between February and April 2024, 41 across 2023, more than 40 transgender women in 2023, and 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025 from the Attorney General's Office. These are not reconciled in the sources and should be read as separate counts rather than a single series.

Whether the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indictment of July 2023 or the 2016 and 2018 decrees have produced enforcement outcomes in Arauca is not sourced.
